content.overview: Sections 1 and 2 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 establish the Act’s territorial and temporal operation and define the foundational contractual concepts used by the operative provisions. The definitions in section 2 must be read as statutory terms, not as free-standing textbook descriptions.
content.glance: Sections 1 and 2 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 establish the Act’s territorial and temporal operation and define the foundational contractual concepts used by the operative provisions. The definitions in section 2 must be read as statutory terms, not as free-standing textbook descriptions.

sections.heading: Section 1 — Title, extent, commencement and savings
sections.body: Section 1 identifies the enactment as the Indian Contract Act, 1872, states its extent, commencement framework and saving clause. The saving provision preserves specified pre-existing usages, customs, incidents of contract and statutory enactments or provisions not repealed by the Act. The precise statutory text controls the scope of each saving.

sections.heading: Section 2 — Interpretation clause
sections.body: Section 2 supplies the vocabulary for the operative scheme. The principal defined expressions include proposal, promise, promisor, promisee, consideration, agreement, reciprocal promises, void agreement and contract. Each definition should be applied by identifying its statutory ingredients before moving to the operative provision governing the dispute.

sections.heading: Proposal, acceptance, promise and agreement
sections.body: Under section 2, a proposal is an expression of willingness to do or abstain from doing something with a view to obtaining the other person's assent; when the person to whom it is made signifies assent, the proposal becomes a promise. The persons making and accepting the proposal become promisor and promisee respectively. Every promise and every set of promises forming the consideration for each other is an agreement.

sections.heading: Consideration, reciprocal promises and contract
sections.body: Section 2(d) defines consideration by reference to an act, abstinence or promise done, abstained from or promised at the desire of the promisor. Section 2(f) recognises reciprocal promises. Section 2(h) defines contract as an agreement enforceable by law, so an agreement is not automatically a contract merely because assent has occurred.

sections.heading: Void agreement and statutory sequencing
sections.body: Section 2(g) identifies a void agreement as one not enforceable by law. In application, begin with the statutory definitions, then identify whether an agreement exists, and finally examine the later provisions of the Act to determine enforceability, validity or voidness.

examples.title: Illustration — Proposal becomes promise
examples.body: A communicates a willingness to sell specified goods to B at a stated price with the object of obtaining B’s assent. If B signifies assent in accordance with the Act, the proposal becomes a promise within section 2.

examples.title: Boundary case — Agreement is not necessarily a contract
examples.body: Two parties may reach an agreement, yet the arrangement may fail to be enforceable because a later statutory requirement or prohibition applies. Section 2(h) therefore requires the separate inquiry whether the agreement is enforceable by law.

hypotheticals.question: A sends B a communication expressing willingness to sell goods, but the communication is merely an invitation to negotiate. Has a proposal under section 2(a) necessarily been made?
hypotheticals.analysis: Identify whether the communication manifests willingness to do or abstain from doing something with a view to obtaining B’s assent. A communication that merely invites offers does not satisfy that statutory formulation merely because it concerns a possible transaction.

hypotheticals.question: A and B agree on a transaction, but its enforcement is prohibited by a later provision of the Act. Is the arrangement necessarily a contract?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 2(h) requires enforceability by law. The analysis therefore proceeds from the existence of an agreement to the later statutory rule governing enforceability; the label placed on the transaction by the parties is not decisive.

rows.left: Every promise and every set of promises forming consideration for each other is an agreement.
rows.right: An agreement enforceable by law is a contract.

rows.left: Whether the required promises and consideration relationship exist.
rows.right: Whether the agreement is enforceable by law.

rows.left: Establishes the contractual arrangement at the definitional level.
rows.right: Confers the statutory status of an enforceable contract.

rows.right: Arises when the person to whom the proposal is made signifies assent.

rows.right: Result of assent to the proposal.

misconceptions.trap: Treating every commercial communication as a statutory proposal.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the exact section 2(a) formulation and ask whether the communication was made with a view to obtaining assent.

misconceptions.trap: Assuming every agreement is a contract.
misconceptions.correction: Section 2(h) adds the requirement of enforceability by law.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should sections 1–2 be used when analysing a contractual dispute?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: First identify the Act’s operation and any relevant saving under section 1. Then classify the transaction using the section 2 definitions—proposal, promise, consideration, agreement, reciprocal promises, void agreement and contract. Only after that apply the operative provision governing validity or enforcement.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: The definitions provide the statutory sequence for analysing later contractual rules.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What is the central submission when the opposing party conflates agreement with contract?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Section 2 distinguishes the two concepts. An agreement is defined by the statutory promise structure; a contract is an agreement enforceable by law. The Court should therefore determine enforceability under the applicable operative provisions rather than treating assent alone as conclusive.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: The submission is confined to the statutory definitions and their sequencing.

enhancement.definition: Sections 1–2 establish the Act’s operation and statutory vocabulary. Section 2 defines the principal formation and enforceability concepts that later provisions apply.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The Indian Contract Act must be read through its statutory definitions: formation terminology is supplied by section 2, while the legal status of an agreement as a contract depends on enforceability by law.

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 1 establishes the Act’s formal operation and savings. Section 2 then supplies the statutory vocabulary through which the later chapters must be read. A proposal is directed toward obtaining assent; assent converts it into a promise; promises forming the consideration for each other constitute an agreement; and only an agreement enforceable by law is a contract. Consideration is separately defined by section 2(d), while section 2(g) identifies an agreement not enforceable by law as void. The correct method is therefore sequential: classify the communication and promises, identify the agreement, and then test enforceability under the substantive provisions.
examples: A communicates a willingness to sell specified goods to B at a stated price with the object of obtaining B’s assent. If B signifies assent in accordance with the Act, the proposal becomes a promise within section 2.

Two parties may reach an agreement, yet the arrangement may fail to be enforceable because a later statutory requirement or prohibition applies. Section 2(h) therefore requires the separate inquiry whether the agreement is enforceable by law.
